qs.p: Ecologists describe the mosses and lichens that first colonize bare rock as ______ species: they arrive early, tolerate harsh conditions, and gradually build up the soil that allows other plants to replace them.
qs.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
qs.e: Species that arrive first and prepare the ground for later arrivals are called "pioneer" species. "Invasive" species are non-native organisms that spread harmfully; "keystone" species have an outsized effect on an established ecosystem; and "endemic" species are native to only one place. None of those matches arriving first on bare rock.

qs.p: The negotiator's manner throughout the talks was ______: although she conceded nothing of substance, her patience and courtesy kept the other side at the table when the discussions threatened to collapse.
qs.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
qs.e: Patience and courtesy that keep tense talks from collapsing describe a manner intended to soothe and win goodwill: "conciliatory." "Belligerent" (hostile) is the opposite. "Evasive" (avoiding direct answers) and "perfunctory" (done with minimal effort) don't fit someone whose courtesy actively held the talks together.

qs.p: The photographer's early work was largely ______, closely imitating the soft-focus style of the painters she admired; only later did she develop the sharp, documentary approach for which she is now known.
qs.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
qs.e: Work that "closely imitat[es]" others' style is "derivative." "Innovative" is the opposite. "Polemical" (strongly argumentative) and "haphazard" (random, careless) don't describe imitation.

qs.p: The following text is adapted from a short story.Imogen had promised her brother that she would not interfere in his affairs, and she kept that promise for nearly a week. But when his letter arrived, its cheerful sentences betraying a worry he would never have admitted aloud, she packed a bag within the hour.
qs.q: As used in the text, what does the word "betraying" most nearly mean?
qs.e: The brother's cheerful letter unintentionally shows a worry he wouldn't admit. "Betraying" here means revealing something without meaning to. "Deceiving," "abandoning," and "denouncing" belong to the sense of betraying a person, which doesn't fit sentences that expose a feeling.

qs.p: Although the eighteenth-century treatise is written in an ______ style that few modern readers find inviting, economists agree that its arguments anticipated several key ideas of their discipline.
qs.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
qs.e: A style that few readers find inviting is difficult to understand: "abstruse." "Accessible" and "elegant" would make the treatise appealing, removing the contrast set up by "Although." "Anonymous" describes authorship, not style.

qs.p: The word "weed" has no botanical meaning. A dandelion in a manicured lawn is considered a weed, while the same plant grown deliberately for its edible leaves is considered a crop. Ecologists therefore define weeds not by any feature of the plants themselves but by the plants' relationship to human goals: a weed is simply a plant growing where people don't want it.
qs.q: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
c: To argue that dandelions should be grown as crops rather than removed from lawns
To describe the biological features that weeds have in common
To criticize ecologists for using an imprecise definition of "weed"
To explain that a familiar category of plants is defined by human preferences rather than by biology
qs.e: The text shows that the same plant can be a weed or a crop depending on human wishes and concludes that "weed" is defined by people's goals. It doesn't recommend growing dandelions, explicitly denies that weeds share defining biological features, and presents the ecologists' definition approvingly.

qs.p: For centuries, Polynesian navigators crossed thousands of kilometers of open Pacific Ocean without instruments. <u>They read the direction of ocean swells, the points on the horizon where particular stars rose and set, and the flight paths of seabirds that return to land each evening.</u> In 1976, the crew of the replica voyaging canoe Hōkūleʻa used these methods to sail from Hawaii to Tahiti, demonstrating that such long voyages could have been made deliberately rather than by drifting.
qs.q: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
c: It explains why the Hōkūleʻa was built as a replica of an ancient canoe.
It presents an argument that Polynesian voyages happened mainly by drifting.
It describes the navigation methods that the voyage discussed later in the text put to the test.
It describes instruments that Polynesian navigators carried on their voyages.
qs.e: The underlined sentence lists the techniques (swells, stars, birds), and the final sentence describes the 1976 voyage that used "these methods" successfully. It says nothing about why a replica was built, the voyage showed the opposite of drifting, and the first sentence states that navigators used no instruments.

qs.p: Text 1Many museum educators favor interactive touchscreens in galleries. The screens, they argue, help visitors learn by letting them explore information about the artworks at their own pace and according to their own interests.Text 2In a study at three art museums, researcher Pilar Duarte found that visitors who used gallery touchscreens spent more time at the screens but less time looking at the artworks themselves, and afterward remembered fewer details about the works than visitors who read printed labels did. Duarte suggests that the screens may compete with, rather than support, visitors' attention to the objects on display.
qs.q: Based on the texts, how would Duarte (Text 2) most likely respond to the educators' argument in Text 1?
c: She would argue that the screens may draw attention away from the artworks, undercutting the learning the educators expect.
She would agree that the screens help visitors remember more about the artworks than printed labels do.
She would argue that visitors should not be allowed to explore information at their own pace.
She would claim that printed labels are more interesting to visitors than touchscreens are.
qs.e: The educators claim screens aid learning; Duarte found screen users looked at the art less and remembered less, and she suggests screens compete for attention. That directly challenges the educators' expectation. Her results contradict choice B, she doesn't object to self-paced exploration as such, and she reports memory and viewing time, not which format visitors found more interesting.

qs.p: The following text is adapted from a novel.For forty years Teodor had repaired other people's violins, coaxing warmth back into cracked spruce and loosened seams. His own instrument, a battered fiddle his father had given him, hung untouched on the workshop wall. When customers asked why he never played it, he said he was too busy. In truth, he was afraid that after so long it would no longer answer him.
qs.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
c: Teodor prefers repairing violins to playing them because he dislikes music.
Teodor avoids playing his own violin because he fears that, after so many years, playing it would disappoint him.
Teodor believes his father's violin is too damaged to be repaired.
Teodor has no time to play his violin because his repair work keeps him busy.
qs.e: The last sentence reveals Teodor's true reason: fear that the instrument, or his connection to it, would "no longer answer him." His claim of being "too busy" is presented as an excuse ("In truth…"). Nothing says the violin is beyond repair or that he dislikes music.

qs.p: Each year, a tree adds a growth ring to its trunk. In wet years the rings tend to be wide, and in dry years narrow, so trees in the same region share a distinctive sequence of wide and narrow rings. By matching the ring pattern in a beam from an old building to patterns in trees whose ages are known, researchers can determine the year in which the beam's tree was cut down.
qs.q: According to the text, how can researchers determine when a timber in an old building was cut?
c: By identifying the species of tree from which the timber came
By counting the timber's rings and subtracting that number from the current year
By measuring how much moisture remains in the timber
By matching the timber's sequence of wide and narrow rings to ring patterns from trees of known age
qs.e: The last sentence describes the method: match the beam's ring pattern to patterns from trees of known age. Simply counting rings gives the tree's age, not the year it was cut; and the text doesn't mention measuring moisture or identifying species.

qs.p: Psychologist Elif Demir hypothesizes that people are more likely to achieve long-term goals when they break those goals into small, specific steps than when they set only a general goal.
qs.q: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Demir's hypothesis?
c: Participants who wrote down specific weekly steps toward a fitness goal were more likely to have reached the goal after six months than participants who set only the general goal.
Most participants in the study said that they preferred setting general goals to setting specific steps.
Participants who set general goals spent less time planning than participants who set specific steps.
Participants who set fitness goals reported feeling more motivated on the day they set them than on later days.
qs.e: The hypothesis compares how often goals are achieved under two approaches. Only the finding in choice A compares actual achievement between people who used specific steps and those who didn't. The others concern momentary motivation, planning time, or preferences, none of which shows which approach leads to success.

qs.p: In Percy Bysshe Shelley's 1818 poem "Ozymandias," a traveler describes a ruined statue of an ancient king in the desert. The poem suggests that the king's proud inscription has become ironic, since nothing of the works he boasted of has survived.
qs.q: Which quotation from the poem most effectively illustrates the claim?
c: "I met a traveller from an antique land"
"'My name is Ozymandias, King of Kings; / Look on my Works, ye Mighty, and despair!'"
"Nothing beside remains. Round the decay / Of that colossal Wreck, boundless and bare / The lone and level sands stretch far away."
"Two vast and trunkless legs of stone / Stand in the desert"
qs.e: The irony arises from the gap between the boast and what is left. Choice C shows that nothing remains but empty sand around the wreck, which makes the boast ironic. The inscription itself (choice B) is the boast, not evidence of the irony; the other quotations introduce the traveler and the statue without showing that his works have vanished.

qs.p:
Electricity Generated from Wind (terawatt-hours)
Region20152022
North120180
South80150
East45100
West3095
An energy analyst claims that the West region, which generated the least wind electricity of the four regions in 2015, had the greatest proportional growth in wind generation from 2015 to 2022.
qs.q: Which choice best describes data from the table that support the analyst's claim?
c: West's wind generation rose from 30 to 95 terawatt-hours, more than tripling, while no other region's generation reached even two and a half times its 2015 level.
South's wind generation increased by 70 terawatt-hours, more than any other region's.
North generated more wind electricity than any other region in both 2015 and 2022.
East's wind generation more than doubled, rising from 45 to 100 terawatt-hours.
qs.e: Proportional growth compares each region's 2022 output with its own 2015 output. West grew by a factor of 95/30 ≈ 3.2; East ≈ 2.2, South ≈ 1.9, North 1.5. Choice A shows West's growth was largest. South's 70-TWh increase is the largest absolute gain, which is a different measure; the other choices don't compare proportional growth across all regions.

qs.p: In laboratory tests, a new antibiotic killed 99 percent of a particular bacterial strain within a few hours. In patients infected with the same strain, however, the drug was far less effective. Researchers then discovered that the drug binds tightly to certain proteins in human blood, leaving relatively little of it free to act on bacteria. This discovery suggests that ______
qs.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
c: laboratory tests of antibiotics are generally more accurate than tests in patients.
the antibiotic would be equally effective in patients if they took a smaller dose.
the bacterial strain in patients was different from the strain tested in the laboratory.
the difference between the laboratory results and the results in patients may be explained in part by something present in blood but absent from the laboratory tests.
qs.e: Blood proteins tie up much of the drug, so less is available to kill bacteria in patients than in the lab, which explains the gap. The text says the strain was the same, binding would make a smaller dose less effective, and nothing supports a general claim about which tests are more accurate.

qs.p: Historians have long debated whether the Norse settlement at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland, dating to about 1000 CE, was occupied for many years or only briefly. Archaeologists excavating the site found relatively little household refuse, almost no graves, and little evidence that the buildings' floors or walls had ever been repaired. These findings suggest that ______
qs.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
c: the settlers were especially careful to bury their dead far from the settlement.
the settlement was occupied for a relatively short time.
the settlement was occupied continuously for several centuries.
the buildings at the site were constructed after the settlers left.
qs.e: Long occupation would leave large refuse heaps, burials, and signs of repairs as buildings aged. Finding little of each points to a brief stay. Centuries of continuous occupation contradict the evidence, nothing suggests burials were placed elsewhere, and buildings couldn't have been built after the settlers left.

qs.p: Hummingbirds can hover in place by moving their wings in a figure-eight ______ most other birds cannot hover for more than a few seconds.
qs.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
qs.e: Two independent clauses joined by the coordinating conjunction "but" need a comma before the conjunction, not after it. No comma belongs after "but," and with no conjunction at all the sentence becomes a run-on.

qs.p: Neither of the two prototype engines ______ the manufacturer's final durability test, so the launch of the new aircraft has been postponed.
qs.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
qs.e: "Neither" (meaning "not one") is singular, so it takes the singular verb "has passed." "Engines" is part of the phrase "of the two prototype engines" and doesn't control the verb. The other choices are plural.

qs.p: Ada Lovelace, ______ notes on Charles Babbage's proposed Analytical Engine included what is often called the first computer program, was the daughter of the poet Lord Byron.
qs.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
qs.e: The notes belong to Lovelace, so the possessive relative pronoun "whose" is needed. "Who's" means "who is," "who" isn't possessive, and "which" refers to things rather than people and isn't possessive here.

qs.p: Between 1850 and 1950, the glacier ______ more than two kilometers up its valley, exposing land that had been covered by ice for thousands of years.
qs.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
qs.e: "Between 1850 and 1950" describes a completed period in the past, so the simple past "retreated" is correct. The present, future, and present perfect forms don't fit a finished past time span.

qs.p: Marie Tharp, an American ______ created the first detailed maps of the Atlantic Ocean floor in the 1950s, revealing a vast underwater mountain range.
qs.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
qs.e: "An American geologist" is an appositive that opens with a comma after "Tharp," so it must close with a comma before the verb "created." Leaving it open, closing it with a dash, or using a semicolon (which would separate the subject from its verb) is incorrect.

qs.p: Long considered too dangerous to climb, ______
qs.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
c: the north face of the Eiger, in the Swiss Alps, was first ascended in 1938.
the year 1938 saw the first ascent of the Eiger's north face, in the Swiss Alps.
the first ascent of the Eiger's north face, in the Swiss Alps, happened in 1938.
climbers first ascended the north face of the Eiger, in the Swiss Alps, in 1938.
qs.e: The opening phrase describes something that was considered too dangerous to climb, so that thing must come immediately after the comma: the north face of the Eiger. Climbers, a year, and an ascent were not "considered too dangerous to climb."

qs.p: Most glass is made by melting sand, soda ash, and limestone together. ______ glassmakers often add small amounts of metal compounds to produce colored glass: cobalt yields deep blue, and chromium yields green.
qs.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
qs.e: The second sentence adds further ingredients to the basic recipe in the first. "In addition" signals that. "In contrast" and "Nonetheless" signal opposition, and "Therefore" wrongly implies that adding metals is a consequence of the basic recipe.

qs.p: Early telescopes produced images fringed with false colors, because their glass lenses bent different colors of light by different amounts. ______ in 1668, Isaac Newton built a telescope that gathered light with a curved mirror instead of a lens, avoiding the problem entirely.
qs.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
c: As an illustration of this problem,
qs.e: Newton's mirror telescope was a solution to the color problem described in the first sentence. "To address this problem" makes that relationship explicit. Newton's design wasn't similar to the faulty lenses or an illustration of their problem, and "Nevertheless" would imply he built it despite the problem.

qs.p: The debut novel was rejected by eleven publishers. ______ when it finally appeared in print, it became a bestseller within months.
qs.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
qs.e: Becoming a bestseller contrasts with repeated rejection, so a contrast word is needed: "Yet." "Therefore" implies the rejections caused the success, "Likewise" signals similarity, and "Specifically" signals detail.

qs.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • A popular belief holds that the Great Wall of China can be seen with the naked eye from space.
  • The wall is very long, but in most places it is less than 10 meters wide.
  • Its color closely matches the surrounding terrain.
  • Astronauts in low Earth orbit have reported that they could not see the wall without magnification.
qs.q: The student wants to correct the popular belief about the Great Wall. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: Many people believe that the Great Wall of China can be seen with the naked eye from space.
The Great Wall of China is very long, but in most places it is less than 10 meters wide.
Although many people believe the Great Wall of China is visible to the naked eye from space, astronauts in low Earth orbit have reported that they could not see it without magnification.
The color of the Great Wall of China closely matches the surrounding terrain.
qs.e: Correcting a belief requires stating it and presenting evidence against it. Only choice C does both. Choices B and D give reasons the wall would be hard to see but don't address the belief, and choice A repeats the belief without correcting it.

qs.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • Most writing systems developed gradually over many centuries.
  • The Korean alphabet, Hangul, was created by scholars working under King Sejong and introduced in the 1440s.
  • The shapes of some Hangul letters reflect the position of the mouth when making the sound.
  • The Cherokee syllabary was created by Sequoyah and completed in 1821.
  • Each Cherokee symbol represents a syllable.
qs.q: The student wants to emphasize a similarity between Hangul and the Cherokee syllabary. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: The shapes of some Hangul letters reflect the position of the mouth when making the sound.
Unlike most writing systems, which developed gradually over centuries, both Hangul and the Cherokee syllabary were deliberately created at a specific time by identifiable people.
Hangul was introduced in the 1440s, while the Cherokee syllabary was completed in 1821.
Each symbol in the Cherokee syllabary represents a syllable.
qs.e: Only choice B names both systems and identifies what they share: deliberate creation rather than gradual development. Choice C contrasts their dates, and choices A and D describe a feature of one system only.

qs.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • In 2015, scientists announced the discovery of fossils of a previously unknown human relative, Homo naledi.
  • The fossils were found in the Rising Star cave system in South Africa.
  • More than 1,500 fossil elements from at least fifteen individuals were recovered.
  • This is one of the largest collections of fossils of a single hominin species ever found in Africa.
qs.q: The student wants to emphasize the size of the discovery. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: Scientists discovered fossils of a human relative in a South African cave system.
Homo naledi fossils were found in the Rising Star cave system in South Africa.
The more than 1,500 Homo naledi fossil elements recovered from the Rising Star cave system make up one of the largest collections of a single hominin species ever found in Africa.
In 2015, scientists announced the discovery of Homo naledi, a previously unknown human relative.
qs.e: Emphasizing size requires the quantity and its significance. Choice C gives the number of fossil elements and notes that it is one of the largest such collections. The others report the discovery or its location without conveying its scale.

qs.p: The diplomat's statement was carefully ______, worded so that each side in the dispute could read it as a concession to its own position.
qs.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
qs.e: A statement that each side can read in its own favor is open to more than one interpretation: "equivocal." "Unambiguous" is the opposite, "vitriolic" (bitterly harsh) doesn't fit a statement meant to please both sides, and "impromptu" (unrehearsed) contradicts "carefully … worded."

qs.p: Far from being ______, the city's new building regulations were the product of years of consultation with engineers, residents, and builders.
qs.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
qs.e: "Far from being ______" requires a word that contrasts with years of consultation, so the blank must mean hasty: "precipitate." "Deliberate," "exhaustive," and "collaborative" all agree with years of consultation, so they eliminate the contrast.

qs.p: Although medieval cathedral builders lacked modern engineering theory, their designs were remarkably ______: walls and flying buttresses carried the weight of the stone vaults so efficiently that many of these structures still stand eight centuries later.
qs.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
qs.e: Designs that carried weight efficiently enough to stand for eight centuries were structurally "sound." "Ornate" (heavily decorated) describes appearance, not stability. "Provisional" (temporary) contradicts the buildings' longevity, and "idiosyncratic" (peculiar) doesn't explain why they still stand.

qs.p: The following text is adapted from an essay on gardening.A garden is never finished. Each season qualifies the last: the spring planting that seemed so bold is softened by summer's overgrowth, and autumn reveals what the gardener's plans had failed to take into account.
qs.q: As used in the text, what does the word "qualifies" most nearly mean?
qs.e: Each season changes or limits the effect of the season before: summer softens spring's boldness, and autumn exposes spring's oversights. That is "qualifies" in the sense of modifies. "Certifies" and "entitles" belong to the sense of meeting requirements, and "describes" doesn't capture the idea of change.

qs.p: The physicist was ______ about her experiment's early results; rather than announcing a discovery, she cautioned that the signal might be an artifact of the equipment and called for independent replication.
qs.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
qs.e: Cautioning that the signal might be an error and asking for replication shows careful, cautious judgment: "circumspect." "Exuberant" (enthusiastic) is the opposite. She takes the results seriously enough to seek replication, so she is neither "dismissive" nor "indifferent."

qs.p: The "Mozart effect," the idea that listening to classical music makes people smarter, became popular in the 1990s after a study reported that college students performed better on a spatial reasoning task after listening to a Mozart sonata. In that study, however, the improvement lasted only about fifteen minutes. Later researchers found that students performed similarly well after listening to other music they enjoyed, suggesting that the effect reflected a temporary lift in mood or alertness rather than any special property of Mozart's music.
qs.q: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
c: To argue that listening to Mozart's music has no effect of any kind on people
To describe the spatial reasoning tasks used in studies of music and intelligence
To explain how later research cast doubt on a popular interpretation of an earlier study's results
To recommend that students listen to music they enjoy before taking tests
qs.e: The text presents a popular belief and its source, then explains how later research suggested a more ordinary explanation (mood or alertness). It doesn't deny any effect (a temporary one remains), doesn't describe the tasks in detail, and makes no recommendation.

qs.p: The following text is adapted from a novel.For thirty years the bakery on Calle Mayor had opened at five o'clock. The baker's son, who took over after his father died, kept the same hours, the same recipes, even the same chipped sign above the door. Customers agreed that nothing had changed. Only the son knew that each morning he stood for a long moment before lighting the ovens, waiting for an instruction that no longer came.
qs.q: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
c: It describes customers' complaints about changes at a bakery.
It describes how a business appears unchanged to outsiders and then reveals a private grief beneath that appearance.
It contrasts a father's baking methods with his son's new methods.
It traces the history of a bakery from its founding to its closing.
qs.e: The text first establishes continuity (same hours, recipes, and sign; customers see no change) and then turns to the son's private moment of waiting for his late father's instruction. It doesn't cover the bakery's founding or closing, the son kept his father's methods, and customers praise rather than complain.

qs.p: Text 1Some ecologists argue that the reintroduction of wolves to Yellowstone National Park in 1995 set off a "trophic cascade." By preying on elk and changing where elk grazed, the wolves allowed willows and aspens along the park's streams to recover from decades of overbrowsing.Text 2Ecologist Mateo Rivas agrees that streamside vegetation has recovered in parts of Yellowstone since 1995 but argues that wolves deserve less credit than they often receive. Elk numbers also fell because of drought, hunting outside the park, and growing populations of bears and cougars. And in many areas willows remain suppressed, Rivas notes, because beavers, whose dams once raised water levels along streams, have not returned.
qs.q: Based on the texts, how would Rivas (Text 2) most likely respond to the ecologists' argument in Text 1?
c: He would argue that it attributes to wolves a recovery that also depends on several other factors.
He would argue that streamside vegetation in Yellowstone has not recovered at all since 1995.
He would claim that bears and cougars have harmed the recovery of willows and aspens.
He would agree that wolves alone explain the changes in Yellowstone's vegetation.
qs.e: Rivas accepts that some recovery occurred but lists other causes of the elk decline (drought, hunting, other predators) and another factor limiting willows (missing beavers). So he thinks the cascade argument gives wolves too much credit. He explicitly says vegetation has recovered in parts of the park, rejects "wolves alone," and presents bears and cougars as reducing elk, which would help vegetation rather than harm it.

qs.p: The "tragedy of the commons" describes how people who share a resource, such as a pasture, may each take more than is sustainable until the resource is ruined for everyone. Political economist Elinor Ostrom, however, documented many communities, including Swiss alpine villages, Japanese forest villages, and Spanish irrigation districts, that managed shared resources sustainably for centuries. Their success, she found, depended on rules that the users developed themselves, such as clear boundaries, monitoring by members of the community, and penalties that increased with repeated violations.
qs.q: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
c: Ostrom found that Swiss villages managed their pastures more successfully than Spanish districts managed their irrigation systems.
Ostrom argued that shared resources are always overused unless they are divided into private property.
Ostrom concluded that the tragedy of the commons occurs only in modern societies.
Ostrom's research showed that communities can avoid overusing shared resources when the users themselves create and enforce suitable rules.
qs.e: The text sets up the "tragedy" idea and then presents Ostrom's counterevidence: long-lasting communities that succeeded through rules they made and enforced themselves. She showed overuse isn't inevitable (contradicting choice B), didn't rank the communities, and drew no conclusion about modern versus older societies.

qs.p: The following text is from Charles Dickens's 1859 novel A Tale of Two Cities.It was the best of times, it was the worst of times, it was the age of wisdom, it was the age of foolishness, it was the epoch of belief, it was the epoch of incredulity, it was the season of Light, it was the season of Darkness, it was the spring of hope, it was the winter of despair.
qs.q: Based on the text, how does the narrator characterize the period being described?
c: As an era that people looked back on with nostalgia
As an era of unrelieved despair and darkness
As an era defined by sharp contradictions
As an era of steady progress toward wisdom and hope
qs.e: Every clause pairs an idea with its opposite (best/worst, wisdom/foolishness, belief/incredulity, Light/Darkness, hope/despair), so the period is characterized by contradiction. Choices B and D each keep only one half of every pair, and nothing in the excerpt mentions nostalgia.

qs.p: A large circular enclosure of stacked stones stands in an arid region of the Sahara that was once grassland. Archaeologist Nadia Ferhat claims that the enclosure was built to hold herds of cattle.
qs.q: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Ferhat's claim?
c: The enclosure's walls are high enough to prevent cattle from escaping.
Rock paintings in the region depict herds of cattle.
Cattle bones dating to the same period have been found at a settlement a few kilometers away.
Soil inside the enclosure shows no elevated levels of phosphate, a chemical that builds up wherever large numbers of animals are kept.
qs.e: If cattle had been kept inside, their waste would have enriched the soil with phosphate; finding no such enrichment undercuts the claim. The other findings (cattle nearby, walls tall enough, cattle in local art) are all consistent with the claim and would tend to support it.

qs.p: A student studying climate on Mount Kessel claims that average annual temperature on the mountain falls by roughly 6°C for every 1,000 meters of elevation gained.
qs.q: Which choice best describes data from the graph that support the student's claim?
c: The station at 1,000 meters had an average temperature of about 14°C, and the station at 2,000 meters had an average temperature of about 8°C.
The station at 500 meters had the highest average temperature of the six stations.
The station at 3,000 meters had the lowest average temperature, about 2°C.
The stations ranged in elevation from 500 meters to 3,000 meters.
qs.e: The claim describes a rate: about 6°C cooler per 1,000 meters. Choice A gives two stations exactly 1,000 meters apart whose temperatures differ by 14 − 8 = 6°C, directly illustrating the rate. The other choices describe single stations or the elevation range, which can't establish a rate of change.

qs.p: In Charlotte Brontë's 1847 novel Jane Eyre, Jane declares to Mr. Rochester that she is free to act on her own decisions.
qs.q: Which quotation from the novel most effectively illustrates the claim?
c: "Do you think, because I am poor, obscure, plain, and little, I am soulless and heartless?"
"I am no bird; and no net ensnares me: I am a free human being with an independent will, which I now exert to leave you."
"I would always rather be happy than dignified."
qs.e: The claim has two parts: a declaration of freedom and the will to act on it. Choice B calls Jane "a free human being with an independent will" and says she is exercising that will. The famous "Reader, I married him" reports an outcome, "rather be happy than dignified" states a preference, and choice A asserts her feeling and worth rather than her freedom to decide.

qs.p: When people estimate how many others share their opinions, they tend to overestimate, a tendency psychologists call the false consensus effect. In a recent study, researchers found that the effect was considerably weaker among people who regularly discussed issues with others who held opposing views. If this finding reflects a causal relationship, then ______
qs.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
c: people who discuss issues with those who disagree are more likely to change their own opinions.
people who rarely discuss issues tend to underestimate how many others share their views.
encouraging people to discuss issues with those who disagree with them might help them judge more accurately how widely their own opinions are shared.
the false consensus effect would disappear entirely if people stopped discussing issues.
qs.e: If talking with people who disagree causes the effect to weaken, then promoting such conversations should make people's estimates more accurate. The study says nothing about opinion change, implies that stopping discussion would make the effect stronger rather than eliminate it, and describes overestimation, not underestimation.

qs.p: Biologists measured anole lizards on two Caribbean islands shortly before a major hurricane struck and measured the surviving lizards again shortly afterward. Compared with the pre-hurricane populations, survivors had larger toe pads and longer front limbs. In wind-tunnel tests, lizards with larger toe pads clung to branches longer in high winds. These findings suggest that ______
qs.q: Which choice most logically completes the text?
c: the lizards' toe pads grew larger in response to the high winds during the hurricane.
lizards with longer front limbs are more common on islands that rarely experience hurricanes.
the hurricane had no lasting effect on the lizard populations of the two islands.
the hurricane may have acted as a selective pressure, favoring traits that helped lizards hold on in strong winds.
qs.e: Survivors differed from the original population in traits that, according to the wind-tunnel tests, improve grip in high winds, which suggests the storm removed lizards less able to hold on. The survivors were measured shortly afterward, too soon for toes to grow; the text compares no islands by hurricane frequency; and a shift in traits is itself a lasting effect.

qs.p: The cave expedition had three ______ to map the passages, to catalog the animals living there, and to collect samples of the mineral formations.
qs.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
qs.e: "The cave expedition had three aims" is a complete clause, and the list that follows specifies those aims. A colon introduces such a list. A semicolon requires an independent clause after it, no punctuation runs the list into "aims," and "aims that" creates an ungrammatical clause.

qs.p: The city's oldest bridge and its newest tunnel ______ designed by the same engineering firm, nearly a century apart.
qs.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
qs.e: Two subjects joined by "and" ("bridge and … tunnel") form a plural subject, which requires the plural verb "were." The other choices are singular.

qs.p: The painting ______ hangs in the museum's main hall was once thought to have been destroyed in a fire.
qs.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
qs.e: "That hangs in the museum's main hall" identifies which painting is meant, so it is essential information and shouldn't be set off with commas. "That" introduces such a clause without commas. Adding a single comma before "that" or "which" separates the subject from its essential description, and "which," followed by a comma breaks the clause.

qs.p: If the Moon were twice as far from Earth as it actually is, the ocean tides it produces ______ much weaker than they are today.
qs.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
qs.e: "If the Moon were…" sets up a hypothetical present situation, which calls for "would" plus a base verb in the result clause: "would be." "Will be" and "are" treat the situation as real, and "had been" belongs to past hypotheticals.

qs.p: Most volcanic eruptions are preceded by swarms of small ______ some, however, occur with almost no warning.
qs.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
qs.e: "Most volcanic eruptions are preceded by swarms of small earthquakes" and "some … occur with almost no warning" are independent clauses. "However" sits inside the second clause and cannot join them, so a semicolon is needed. A comma creates a comma splice, no punctuation creates a run-on, and a comma after "and" is incorrect.

qs.p: Saturn's main rings are enormous, extending hundreds of thousands of kilometers from the ______ they are remarkably thin, in many places only about ten meters thick.
qs.q: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
qs.e: The two independent clauses are joined by the coordinating conjunction "yet," which takes a comma before it and none after. A comma alone creates a comma splice, and placing commas after "yet" is incorrect.

qs.p: Most critics praised the film's cinematography, especially its long, unbroken shots of the desert. Its screenplay, ______ drew sharp criticism for implausible plot twists and stiff dialogue.
qs.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
qs.e: Criticism of the screenplay contrasts with praise for the cinematography, so "by contrast" fits. The screenplay isn't an example of the cinematography, isn't simply another praised feature, and its criticism isn't caused by the praise.

qs.p: The bacterium Thermus aquaticus lives in hot springs at temperatures above 70°C. ______ the enzymes it produces remain stable at high temperatures, a property that makes one of them invaluable for laboratory techniques that require repeated heating.
qs.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
qs.e: An organism that lives in very hot water would be expected to have heat-stable enzymes, so the second sentence follows from the first: "Accordingly." "Nevertheless" implies the stability is surprising, "Instead" signals a replacement, and "Meanwhile" signals simultaneous but unrelated events.

qs.p: Some historians argue that the printing press caused the Protestant Reformation. Others contend that this claim greatly overstates the press's role. ______ few dispute that printed pamphlets helped spread Reformation ideas far faster than handwritten copies could have.
qs.q: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
qs.e: After describing a disagreement, the text notes a point both sides accept despite their differences. "Still" introduces a point that holds in spite of what came before. "Therefore" implies a conclusion drawn from the debate, "For instance" signals an example, and "Similarly" signals another parallel view.

qs.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • The Hubble Space Telescope, launched in 1990, observes mainly in visible and ultraviolet light.
  • The James Webb Space Telescope, launched in 2021, observes mainly in infrared light.
  • As the universe expands, light from very distant galaxies is stretched toward longer, infrared wavelengths.
  • Infrared light can also pass through clouds of dust that block visible light.
qs.q: The student wants to explain why the James Webb Space Telescope can observe some objects that the Hubble Space Telescope cannot. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: As the universe expands, light from very distant galaxies is stretched toward infrared wavelengths.
The Hubble Space Telescope was launched in 1990, and the James Webb Space Telescope was launched in 2021.
The Hubble Space Telescope observes mainly in visible and ultraviolet light.

Because the Webb telescope observes mainly in infrared light, it can detect very distant galaxies whose light has been stretched into infrared wavelengths, as well as objects hidden behind dust that blocks the visible light Hubble observes.
qs.e: An explanation must connect Webb's capability (infrared) to the objects it can see that Hubble can't (stretched light from distant galaxies, objects behind dust). Only choice D makes that connection. The others give launch dates, describe one telescope, or state a fact about light without linking it to either telescope.

qs.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • Some city officials argue that making public transit free would be too costly.
  • In 2020, Luxembourg became the first country to make all public transit free nationwide.
  • Before the change, fares had covered only about 8 percent of the system's operating costs.
  • The government described the lost fare revenue as small relative to the system's total budget.
qs.q: The student wants to respond to the concern that free public transit would be too costly, using Luxembourg as an example. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: Although some officials argue that free transit would be too costly, Luxembourg eliminated fares nationwide in 2020, giving up revenue that had covered only about 8 percent of the system's operating costs.
Before 2020, fares in Luxembourg covered about 8 percent of the public transit system's operating costs.
Some city officials argue that making public transit free would be too costly.
In 2020, Luxembourg became the first country to make all public transit free nationwide.
qs.e: Responding to a concern requires acknowledging it and offering a counterpoint. Choice A states the concern, then shows that in Luxembourg the lost fares were a small share of costs. The other choices present the example, the concern, or the statistic alone without connecting them.

qs.p:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • The Empire State Building is a 102-story skyscraper in New York City.
  • Construction began in March 1930.
  • The building officially opened on May 1, 1931.
  • It remained the world's tallest building until 1970.
qs.q: The student wants to emphasize how quickly the Empire State Building was built. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
c: The Empire State Building remained the world's tallest building until 1970.
Construction of the Empire State Building began in March 1930.
The 102-story Empire State Building opened on May 1, 1931, only about fourteen months after construction began in March 1930.
The Empire State Building is a 102-story skyscraper in New York City.
qs.e: Emphasizing speed requires both the size of the project and the short time it took. Choice C gives the height and the roughly fourteen-month span between the start of construction and the opening. The others mention only its height, its record, or its start date.

qs.q: If 7 − 2x = 3x − 13, what is the value of 5x?
qs.e: Add 2x and 13 to both sides: 20 = 5x. The question asks for 5x itself, so the answer is 20. (Solving for x gives 4, which is a trap.)

qs.q: A plumber charges a fixed fee plus an hourly rate. A 2-hour job costs $190, and a 5-hour job costs $385. What is the plumber's fixed fee?
qs.e: The extra 3 hours cost $385 − $190 = $195, so the hourly rate is $195 ÷ 3 = $65. For the 2-hour job, $190 = fee + 2($65), so the fee is $190 − $130 = $60.

qs.q: A bookstore buys a book from a publisher for $15 and sells it at a price that is 40% greater than what the store paid. What is the selling price of the book, in dollars?
qs.e: A 40% markup means the selling price is 140% of the cost: 1.40 × $15 = $21.

qs.q:
y = 3x − 1
2x + y = 9
If (x, y) is the solution to the system of equations above, what is the value of x?
qs.e: Substitute the first equation into the second: 2x + (3x − 1) = 9, so 5x = 10 and x = 2. (Then y = 5.)

qs.q:
Number of pets01234
Number of students812631
The table shows how many pets each of 30 students has. What is the median number of pets?
qs.e: With 30 values, the median is the average of the 15th and 16th values in order. The first 8 values are 0, and values 9 through 20 are 1. So the 15th and 16th values are both 1, and the median is 1. (Taking the middle of the "number of pets" row, 2, ignores the frequencies.)

qs.q: If (x − 3)2 = 49 and x > 0, what is the value of x?
qs.e: Take square roots: x − 3 = 7 or x − 3 = −7, so x = 10 or x = −4. Since x > 0, x = 10.

qs.q: Which expression is equivalent to (2x − 5)2?
qs.e: (2x − 5)2 = (2x − 5)(2x − 5) = 4x2 − 10x − 10x + 25 = 4x2 − 20x + 25. Squaring each term separately (4x2 + 25 or − 25) leaves out the middle term.

qs.q: The ratio of boys to girls in a robotics club is 3 to 5. If the club has 40 members, how many more girls than boys are in the club?
qs.e: The ratio 3 : 5 splits 40 members into 3 + 5 = 8 equal parts of 5 members each. There are 3 × 5 = 15 boys and 5 × 5 = 25 girls, so there are 25 − 15 = 10 more girls.

qs.q: A rectangle has a length of 12 inches and a diagonal of 13 inches. What is the area of the rectangle, in square inches?
qs.e: The diagonal splits the rectangle into right triangles, so the width is √13² − 12² = √25 = 5. The area is 12 × 5 = 60. (156 multiplies the length by the diagonal.)

qs.q: The scatterplot shows the number of hours each of ten students studied and the student's test score, along with a line of best fit. Based on the line of best fit, which of the following is closest to the predicted test score for a student who studied for 5 hours?
qs.e: Read the dashed line, not the individual points, at 5 hours: it passes through about 82. (The line rises about 6 points per hour from about 52 at 0 hours, and 52 + 6 × 5 = 82.)

qs.q: The function g is defined by g(x) = −2x + 7. If g(a) = −5, what is the value of a?

The mass, in grams, of a radioactive sample x days after it was measured is modeled by f(x) = 400(0.5)x/8. According to the model, how many days does it take for the mass of the sample to be cut in half?
qs.e: The mass is multiplied by 0.5 each time the exponent x/8 increases by 1, which happens every 8 days. So the half-life is 8 days. (200 is the mass remaining after 8 days, not a number of days, and 16 is the time for the mass to fall to a quarter.)

qs.q: Two angles form a linear pair. The measure of one angle is 20° less than 4 times the measure of the other. What is the measure of the larger angle?
qs.e: Angles in a linear pair are supplementary: x + (4x − 20) = 180, so 5x = 200 and x = 40. The larger angle is 4(40) − 20 = 140°.

qs.q: A spinner is divided into 8 equal sections numbered 1 through 8. If the spinner is spun once, what is the probability that it lands on a number that is greater than 5 or even?
qs.e: Numbers greater than 5: 6, 7, 8. Even numbers: 2, 4, 6, 8. Together (counting 6 and 8 only once): 2, 4, 6, 7, 8, which is 5 of 8 sections. The probability is 5/8. Adding 3/8 + 4/8 = 7/8 double-counts 6 and 8.

qs.q: A right circular cylinder has a volume of 72π cubic centimeters and a radius of 3 centimeters. What is the height of the cylinder, in centimeters?
qs.e: V = πr2h, so 72π = π(9)h, giving 9h = 72 and h = 8.

qs.q: A student has $60 to spend on notebooks that cost $4 each and pens that cost $1.50 each. Which of the following combinations of notebooks and pens can the student buy without spending more than $60?
qs.e: Compute each total, 4n + 1.5p: 10 and 14 cost $40 + $21 = $61; 13 and 6 cost $52 + $9 = $61; 9 and 17 cost $36 + $25.50 = $61.50; 12 and 8 cost $48 + $12 = $60. Only 12 notebooks and 8 pens stays within $60.

qs.q: The function f is defined by f(x) = (x − 1)(x + 3)(x − 5). What are the x-intercepts of the graph of y = f(x) in the xy-plane?
qs.e: f(x) = 0 when any factor equals 0: x − 1 = 0, x + 3 = 0, or x − 5 = 0. So the x-intercepts are 1, −3, and 5. The first choice flips the sign of each.

qs.q: From a point on level ground 40 meters from the base of a building, the angle of elevation to the top of the building is θ, where tan θ = 1.5. What is the height of the building, in meters?
qs.e: tan θ = opposite/adjacent = height/40. So height = 40 × 1.5 = 60 meters. (26.7 comes from dividing 40 by 1.5.)

qs.q: The mean of the three numbers x, 2x, and 3x is 18. What is the value of x?
qs.e: The mean is (x + 2x + 3x)/3 = 6x/3 = 2x. Setting 2x = 18 gives x = 9.

qs.q: Brand A sells an 18-ounce jar of peanut butter for $4.50, and Brand B sells a 24-ounce jar for $5.76. How much less per ounce does Brand B cost than Brand A?
qs.e: Brand A: $4.50 ÷ 18 = $0.25 per ounce. Brand B: $5.76 ÷ 24 = $0.24 per ounce. Brand B costs $0.01 less per ounce. ($1.26 is the difference in jar prices, not in unit prices.)

qs.q: In the equation 4(x − 3) + k = 2(2x + 1), k is a constant. For what value of k does the equation have infinitely many solutions?
qs.e: Expand: 4x − 12 + k = 4x + 2. The x-terms already match, so the equation is true for every x exactly when −12 + k = 2, which gives k = 14. Any other value makes the equation false for every x.

qs.q: For positive numbers x and y, x2 + y2 = 41 and xy = 20. What is the value of x + y?
qs.e: (x + y)2 = x2 + 2xy + y2 = 41 + 40 = 81. Since x and y are positive, x + y = 9. (81 is the square of the answer. The numbers are 4 and 5.)

qs.q: What value of x satisfies x + 23 = 2x − 15?
Which expression is equivalent to (x2y−3)2x−1y, where x > 0 and y > 0?
qs.e: The numerator is x4y−6. Dividing by x−1y subtracts exponents: x4 − (−1)y−6 − 1 = x5y−7 = x5/y7. Mishandling the negative exponent on x in the denominator gives x3.

qs.q: The value of a car decreased from $24,000 to $19,440 over two years, decreasing by the same percentage each year. By what percent did the car's value decrease each year? (Disregard the % sign when entering your answer. For example, enter 20 for 20%.)
qs.e: If the value is multiplied by r each year, then 24,000r2 = 19,440, so r2 = 0.81 and r = 0.9. Keeping 90% each year means a 10% decrease. (Dividing the total 19% drop by 2 gives 9.5, which ignores compounding.)

qs.q: The function f is defined by f(x) = 2x2 − 8x + c, where c is a constant. If f(5) = 17, what is the value of f(−1)?
qs.e: The axis of symmetry is x = −(−8)/(2·2) = 2. The inputs 5 and −1 are each 3 units from 2, so f(−1) = f(5) = 17. (Directly: f(5) = 50 − 40 + c = 17 gives c = 7, and f(−1) = 2 + 8 + 7 = 17.)

qs.q: A job offers two salary options, each starting at $40,000 per year. Under Option A, the salary increases by $2,000 each year. Under Option B, the salary increases by 4% each year. After 10 annual increases, which option pays the higher salary, and by approximately how much?
qs.e: Option A: 40,000 + 10(2,000) = $60,000. Option B: 40,000(1.04)<sup>10</sup> ≈ 40,000(1.4802) ≈ $59,210. Option A is higher by about $790. (Exponential growth eventually wins, but not yet after 10 years.)

qs.q: A regular hexagon has sides of length 6. The area of the hexagon can be written as k√3. What is the value of k?
qs.e: A regular hexagon divides into 6 equilateral triangles with side 6. Each has area (√3/4)(6)2 = 9√3. The hexagon's area is 6 × 9√3 = 54√3, so k = 54.

qs.q: What value of x satisfies the equation 1x + 12x = 14?
Every value in a data set is multiplied by 3. Which statement correctly describes how the mean and the standard deviation of the data set change?
c: The mean is multiplied by 3, and the standard deviation does not change.
The mean increases by 3, and the standard deviation is multiplied by 3.
Neither the mean nor the standard deviation changes.
The mean and the standard deviation are both multiplied by 3.
qs.e: Multiplying every value by 3 multiplies the mean by 3. It also stretches every distance from the mean by a factor of 3, so the standard deviation is multiplied by 3. (Adding a constant to every value would shift the mean but leave the standard deviation unchanged.)

qs.q: A circle has a radius of 8 inches. What is the length, in inches, of an arc intercepted by a central angle of 3π4 radians?
qs.e: When the angle θ is in radians, arc length = rθ = 8 × (3π/4) = 6π inches.

qs.q: The polynomial p(x) = x3 − 6x2 + 11x − 6 has three real zeros, one of which is x = 1. What is the largest zero of p?
qs.e: Because 1 is a zero, x − 1 is a factor. Dividing gives p(x) = (x − 1)(x2 − 5x + 6) = (x − 1)(x − 2)(x − 3). The zeros are 1, 2, and 3, so the largest is 3.

qs.q: A cube has a total surface area of 150 square centimeters. What is the volume of the cube, in cubic centimeters?
qs.e: A cube has 6 congruent square faces, so each face has area 150 ÷ 6 = 25 and the edge length is 5. The volume is 5<sup>3</sup> = 125.

qs.q: The graph of y = g(x) is obtained by reflecting the graph of y = 2x across the x-axis and then shifting the result up 3 units. Which equation defines g?
qs.e: Reflecting across the x-axis negates the output: y = −2x. Shifting up 3 adds 3: g(x) = −2x + 3. Replacing x with −x (as in 2−x) reflects across the y-axis instead.

qs.q: An inspector tested a random sample of 200 light bulbs from a factory's production run of 5,000 bulbs and found that 3% of the sample were defective. The margin of error for this estimate is 2 percentage points. Which of the following is a plausible number of defective bulbs in the entire production run?
qs.e: The plausible range for the defect rate is 3% ± 2%, or 1% to 5%. Applied to 5,000 bulbs, that is 50 to 250 defective bulbs. Only 150 lies in that range.

qs.q: If 2x · 4x + 1 = 128, what is the value of x?
qs.e: Rewrite with base 2: 2x · 22x + 2 = 23x + 2, and 128 = 27. So 3x + 2 = 7 and x = 5/3.

qs.q: The function f is defined by f(x) = x2 − 2x − 15. Which of the following equivalent forms of f(x) displays the x-intercepts of the graph of y = f(x) as constants or coefficients?
qs.e: Factored form shows the zeros: (x − 5)(x + 3) = 0 when x = 5 or x = −3. Vertex form (x − 1)2 − 16 displays the vertex, not the intercepts. The other two forms are also equivalent, but the numbers they display (2 and −15, or 3, −1, and −12) are not the intercepts; for example, x = 3 gives (0)(4) − 12 = −12, not 0.

qs.q: In triangle ABC, AB = AC and the measure of angle A is 40°. Point D lies on side AC so that segment BD bisects angle ABC. What is the measure of angle BDC?
qs.e: Since AB = AC, angles B and C are equal: (180° − 40°)/2 = 70° each. BD bisects angle B, so angle DBC = 35°. In triangle BDC: angle BDC = 180° − 35° − 70° = 75°. (105° is angle ADB, its supplement.)

qs.q: How many liters of a 10% acid solution must be mixed with 30 liters of a 40% acid solution to produce a solution that is 25% acid?
qs.e: Acid is conserved: 0.10x + 0.40(30) = 0.25(x + 30). Then 0.10x + 12 = 0.25x + 7.5, so 4.5 = 0.15x and x = 30. (Sense check: 25% is exactly halfway between 10% and 40%, so equal amounts are needed.)

qs.q: How many solutions does the equation |x − 3| = 2x have?
qs.e: Case 1: x − 3 = 2x gives x = −3, but then the right side is −6, and an absolute value can't equal a negative number, so −3 is not a solution. Case 2: −(x − 3) = 2x gives 3 = 3x, so x = 1; check: |1 − 3| = 2 = 2(1). There is exactly one solution.

qs.q: If sin θ = 513 and π2 < θ < π, what is the value of cos θ?
qs.e: From sin<sup>2</sup>θ + cos<sup>2</sup>θ = 1: cos<sup>2</sup>θ = 1 − 25/169 = 144/169, so cos θ = ±12/13. In the second quadrant (between π/2 and π), cosine is negative, so cos θ = −12/13. (−5/12 is tan θ.)

qs.q: What is the area of the triangle in the xy-plane with vertices at (1, 1), (7, 1), and (4, 9)?
qs.e: The side from (1, 1) to (7, 1) is horizontal with length 6. The third vertex is 9 − 1 = 8 units above that side, so the height is 8. Area = (1/2)(6)(8) = 24.

qs.q: A company's cost, in dollars, to produce n shirts is C(n) = 25n + 300. The company produces shirts at a rate of 40 shirts per hour, so n(t) = 40t, where t is the number of hours of production. Which function gives the cost in terms of t?
qs.e: Substitute n = 40t into C: 25(40t) + 300 = 1,000t + 300. Adding 25 and 40 (to get 65) or multiplying 300 by 40 doesn't represent the composition.

qs.q: In the xy-plane, the circle with equation (x − 3)2 + (y − k)2 = 25, where k is a constant, passes through the points (0, 8) and (6, 0). What is the value of k?
qs.e: From (6, 0): 9 + k2 = 25, so k = 4 or −4. From (0, 8): 9 + (8 − k)2 = 25, so 8 − k = ±4 and k = 4 or 12. The only value satisfying both is k = 4.
